items.name: the surface and its meaning here, with the evidence
its role: the qualifier and what it gives the characteristic
whether the act is a refusal or a pursuit
what the act is directed at or against
the outward act the inner act produces, where the verse states one
the other party and the sequence, with the route
how it appears here: the circumstance of the verse
the operation as an action description (who or what does what), its mode, the primary one
the chain of operations the verse links in sequence
a typed flag: data-quality, or discovery for the claims process

verses.text: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is a demand put as a question: what the Lord asks of Israel (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').
Fear here is reverent awe before the Lord (tree H3372 1a3 'to fear, reverence, honour, respect').
Ways here is the figure for the course of a life lived toward the Lord (tree H1870 1e 'of course of life (fig.)').
Love here is love of a person toward God (tree H0157 1a3 'human love for or to God').
Serve here is the service of the Lord (tree H5647 1a4 'to serve (God)').
Heart and soul together say that the service is given with the whole inner seat (tree H3824 1a2 'heart (of man)'; H5315 1a 'the inner being of man').
The Lord's asking is a pursuit: he looks for something from Israel.
The fear is required, a pursuit set before Israel.
The walking in his ways is required, a pursuit set before Israel.
The love is required, a pursuit set before Israel.
The service is required, a pursuit set before Israel.
What the Lord asks is four things: to fear him, to walk in his ways, to love him and to serve him.
The one feared is the Lord their God.
The ways are the Lord's: the course he sets for them.
The one loved is the Lord.
The one served is the Lord their God.
Walking is the outward act of the ways: living by the course the Lord sets.
The Lord asks; Israel is the one asked.
Israel is to fear the Lord, who is the one feared.
Israel is to walk in the Lord's ways and to love him.
Israel is to serve the Lord.
The speaker turns to this after recalling forty days on the mountain and the Lord's unwillingness to destroy them (Deu 10:10-11).
The Lord asks Israel for four things.
Israel is to fear the Lord.
Israel is to live by the Lord's ways.
Israel is to love the Lord.
Israel is to serve the Lord with the whole inner seat.
The one question is answered by four infinitives: to fear, to walk, to love and to serve.
The four are one requirement, not four separate ones.
The question states what the Lord requires; it is not asked to gain information.
Discovery: other verses join fear, love, walking and service; the claims process tests how the four relate across them.

verses.text: then you shall inquire and make search and ask diligently. And behold, if it be true and certain that such an abomination has been done among you,

reference_observations.obs_text: The first verb is to inquire after a matter with care, a seeking out (tree H1875 1a2 'to consult, enquire of, seek').
The second verb is to search a matter through (tree H2713 1a3 'to examine thoroughly').
The third verb puts questions to people (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
Diligently, as the ESV renders it, makes the asking thorough: the verb is the Hiphil of the word for good (tree H3190 1b '(Hiphil)'), so it is done well.
The inquiring is a pursuit: the reader is told to go after the facts.
The searching is a pursuit: the matter is to be examined to its end.
The asking is a pursuit: people are to be questioned until the report is settled.
What the inquiring is into is the report of a wicked thing done in the city.
What the searching examines is whether the report holds.
What the asking draws out is what was done among them.
The one addressed is told to inquire, search and ask; the people of the city are those whose doing is inquired into.
The reader has heard (Deu 13:12-13) that worthless men have drawn the people of a city to serve other gods.
The reader is told to inquire into the report.
The reader is told to search the matter out.
The reader is told to question people carefully.
Three verbs of inquiry lead to the test of the report: it must prove true, sure and a real abomination done among them.
The three verbs form a stepped investigation, each going further than the last.
Discovery: what is to be done when the report is found true is in the next verses (Deu 13:15-16); the passage is needed.

verses.text: just as you desired of the Lord your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, ‘Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die.’

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is a request made of the Lord, an asking for something to be granted (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').
Hear here is perceiving by ear the Lord's voice (tree H8085 1a1 'to hear (perceive by ear)').
See here is taking in the sight of the great fire with the eyes (tree H7200 1a1 'to see').
Die here is the dying the people fear (tree H4191 1a1 'to die').
The asking is a pursuit: the people made a request of the Lord.
The negator makes the hearing something they ask to be spared: a refusal.
The same negator makes the seeing something they ask to be spared: a refusal.
The dying is what they seek to avoid: a refusal of death.
What they asked of the Lord is recorded in what they said, a plea not to be exposed to him.
What they asked not to hear is the voice of the Lord.
What they asked not to see is the great fire.
The people asked; the Lord is the one asked.
The people ask not to hear or see the Lord's voice and fire; the Lord is the one whose presence is meant.
The people are the ones who fear to die; the Lord's presence is what they fear.
The speaker recalls the assembly at Horeb while speaking of the prophet to come (Deu 18:15-16).
The people made their request of the Lord at Horeb.
They asked not to hear the Lord's voice again.
They asked not to see the great fire again.
They feared that they would die.
They asked at Horeb; they said let us not hear or see; they gave their dying as the reason.
The voice and the fire are what they fear will bring death: his presence is too much for them.
Discovery: the Lord's answer to the request is in the next verse (Deu 18:17); the passage is needed.

verses.text: Remember the days of old; consider the years of many generations; ask your father, and he will show you, your elders, and they will tell you.

reference_observations.obs_text: Remember is calling the past to mind (tree H2142 1a 'to remember, recall').
Consider is giving heed to and discerning the years (tree H0995 1a3 'to observe, mark, give heed to, distinguish, consider').
The verb is putting a question to those who know (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
The remembering is commanded as a pursuit: the people are to go back to the days of old.
The considering is commanded as a pursuit: the years are to be weighed.
The asking is commanded as a pursuit: the people are to seek what the old can tell.
What is to be remembered is the days of old.
What is to be considered is the years of many generations.
The answer of the ones asked is a showing and a telling.
The people are told to ask; their father and their elders are the ones asked.
The charge follows the words that the people have repaid the Lord foolishly (Deu 32:5-6).
The people are told to call the days of old to mind.
The people are told to weigh the years of many generations.
The people are told to ask their father and elders, who will show and tell.
Remember, consider, ask; and the father will show and the elders will tell.
The father and the elders are the ones who hold what the people are to learn.
Discovery: what the father and elders will tell is not stated here; the verses that follow (Deu 32:8-9) are the passage to read.

verses.text: “ For ask now of the days that are past, which were before you, since the day that God created man on the earth, and ask from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a great thing as this has ever happened or was ever heard of.

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is an imperative to enquire, to put the question to past time and to the whole of heaven (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
Heard is hearing of something, news of it reaching the ear (tree H8085 1a2 'to hear of or concerning').
The asking is a pursuit: the people are sent to search for an answer.
What is asked of is the days that are past and the span of heaven, and what is asked is whether such a great thing has happened.
What might have been heard of is such a great thing as this.
The speaker commands the people to ask; the days and the span of heaven are what they are to ask.
The speaker follows the promise of return and mercy (Deu 4:30-31) by sending Israel to ask.
The people are told to ask of past days and of heaven's ends whether anything like this has happened.
The question put is whether such a thing was ever heard of.
The people ask of the past and of heaven whether such a thing has happened or been heard of.
The asking is set as a test by comparison, the whole of time and heaven searched for the like.
Discovery: what the great thing is, the passage gives in the verses after (Deu 4:33-34).

verses.text: “When your son asks you in time to come, ‘What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the Lord our God has commanded you?’

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is a son's question about the meaning of the Lord's commands (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
The son's asking is a pursuit of the meaning of the commands.
What the son will ask about is the meaning of the testimonies, the statutes and the rules.
The son asks; the father is the one asked; the Lord is the one who gave the commands asked about.
The question arises from what the Lord has commanded, after the people are told to do what is right and good (Deu 6:18).
In time to come the son will ask his father the meaning of the commands.
The son asks, and the father is then to answer (Deu 6:21).
The commands are expected to raise the child's question, so that the answer can be given.
Discovery: the answer to be given is in the next verses (Deu 6:21-22); the passage is needed.

verses.text: Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry.”

reference_observations.obs_text: Speak here is a command given to be spoken out to the people (tree H1696 1 'to speak, declare, converse, command, promise, warn, threaten, sing').
The verb is asking for something as a favour (tree H7592 1a2 'to ask (as a favour), borrow'), here from neighbours.
The asking is a pursuit: each is to seek goods from the neighbour.
What is to be spoken goes to the people.
What is asked for is silver and gold articles.
Moses is to speak; the people are the ones addressed.
Every man asks his neighbour and every woman her neighbour; the neighbours are the ones asked.
The Lord is speaking to Moses before the last plague, saying that Pharaoh will let the people go (Exo 11:1).
Moses is told to speak in the hearing of the people.
The people are to ask their neighbours for goods.
Moses speaks in the hearing of the people so that they ask their neighbours.
The asking is laid on every man and woman, not on a chosen few.
Discovery: whether the asking is met with a gift or a loan, the claims process tests against the other verses of this asking.

verses.text: The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing.

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is asking for something as a favour (tree H7592 1a2 'to ask (as a favour), borrow'), here the Egyptians are asked for silver, gold and clothing.
The asking is a pursuit: the people sought goods from the Egyptians.
What they asked for is silver and gold articles and clothing.
The word they followed in asking is what Moses told them.
The people of Israel asked; the Egyptians were the ones asked; Moses is the one whose word they followed.
The Egyptians are urging the people out of the land in haste (Exo 12:33) as the people leave.
The people of Israel asked the Egyptians for goods, as they had been told.
The people did as Moses told them: they asked the Egyptians for goods.
The asking is done under the word given by Moses and not on the people's own initiative.
Discovery: how the Egyptians answered the asking is not stated in this verse; the passage gives it.

verses.text: And the Lord had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.

reference_observations.obs_text: Favour here is the regard the Egyptians held for the people (tree H2580 1b 'favour, acceptance').
The verb is in the causative stem: the Egyptians let the people ask successfully, they grant (tree H7592 1d2 'to grant, make over to, let (one) ask (successfully)').
In the sight of the Egyptians says where the favour stands: in their eyes (tree H5869 1a2 'as showing mental qualities').
The favour was given to the people.
What is granted is whatever the people asked.
The favour came by the Lord's giving.
The granting ends in plunder: the Egyptians are stripped.
The Lord gives the favour; the people receive it; it is held by the Egyptians.
The Egyptians grant what is asked; the people are the ones who asked.
The Egyptians have been urging the people out in haste (Exo 12:33) and the people have asked them for goods (Exo 12:35).
The Lord had given the people favour with the Egyptians.
The Egyptians granted the people what they asked.
The Lord gave favour, so that the Egyptians granted what was asked; thus the people plundered them.
Discovery: the same favour is spoken of in Exo 3:21 and Exo 11:3; the claims process tests how it is given and what it rests on.

verses.text: And when in time to come your son asks you, ‘ What does this mean?’ you shall say to him, ‘ By a strong hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is a child's question about the meaning of what is done (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
Hand here is the Lord's power by which he acted (tree H3027 1b 'strength, power (fig.)').
Strong gives the hand its measure: a powerful hand, the strength of the Lord's act (tree H2392 'strength').
The asking is a pursuit: the son will seek the meaning.
What the son will ask about is this, what has just been laid down about the firstborn (Exo 13:12-13).
The strong hand acted against Egypt: Israel is brought out of it, out of the house of slavery.
The strong hand shows in what was done: the bringing out.
The son asks; the father is the one asked and is to answer.
The Lord acts by his hand; Israel is the one brought out.
The word is given with the law of the firstborn laid down in the verses before (Exo 13:12-13).
In time to come the son will ask his father what the rite means.
The father is to say that the Lord brought them out of Egypt by his strong hand.
The son asks, the father answers, and the answer is the Lord's bringing out by a strong hand.
The answer to the child's question about the rite is what the Lord did, not an account of the rite itself.
Discovery: the rest of the answer, which ties the rite to the firstborn of Egypt, is in the next verse; the passage is needed.

verses.text: Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent.

reference_observations.obs_text: Kiss here is a greeting of affection between kin (tree H5401 1a 'to kiss', in cluster friendship).
The verb is a mutual enquiry after each other's state (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
The asking is a pursuit on both sides: each seeks word of the other.
The one kissed is his father-in-law.
What they asked of each other is their welfare.
The kiss comes with a bowing down, an outward show of respect.
Moses kisses; his father-in-law is the one kissed.
Each asks the other: Moses and his father-in-law ask one another.
Jethro has come to Moses in the wilderness with Moses' wife and sons (Exo 18:5-6).
Moses kissed his father-in-law.
They asked one another how they fared.
Moses goes out, bows and kisses him; then they ask of each other's welfare and go into the tent.
Moses honours his father-in-law as his senior in this greeting.
Discovery: what each told the other of his welfare is not stated; the passage gives what Moses then told him (Exo 18:8).

verses.text: but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians.”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is asking for something as a favour (tree H7592 1a2 'to ask (as a favour), borrow'), here asking neighbours for goods.
The asking is a pursuit: each woman is to seek goods from her neighbour.
What is asked for is silver and gold articles and clothing.
The asking ends in plunder: the Egyptians are stripped of these things.
Each Israelite woman asks; her neighbour and the Egyptians are the ones asked.
These are God's words of what will happen when the people go out of Egypt (Exo 3:20-21).
Each woman is told to ask her neighbour and the woman in her house for goods.
They ask, they put what they receive on their sons and daughters, and so they plunder the Egyptians.
The favour God gives the people in the sight of the Egyptians is what the asking draws on.
Discovery: what the asking amounts to, a request granted or a borrowing, the claims process tests against the other verses of this asking.

verses.text: Then I asked her, ‘ Whose daughter are you?’ She said, ‘The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor’s son, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question to a person for information (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
The asking is a pursuit: he seeks to learn something from her.
What he asks is whose daughter she is, her family.
The servant asks; Rebekah is the one asked and she answers him.
The servant is telling how it went at the spring, after she had given him and his camels drink (Gen 24:45-46).
The servant asked Rebekah to name her family.
He asked, she named her father and grandfather, and then he gave her the ring and bracelets.
He asks to learn whether she belongs to his master's kin.
Discovery: the purpose behind the question is read from verse 48; the passage is needed to settle it.

verses.text: They said, “Let us call the young woman and ask her.”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question to a person (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for'); the Hebrew has it at her mouth (H6310), so the asking is of her own word, which the English hides.
Calling her gives the asking its setting: she is summoned so that she can be asked herself (tree H7121 1a5 'to summon, invite, call for').
The asking is a pursuit: they propose to seek her answer.
The asking is directed at the young woman herself, at her mouth.
The family propose to ask; the young woman is the one to be asked.
The family answer the servant's request to be sent away (Gen 24:56) by proposing to hear her.
The family propose to summon her and ask her.
They will call the young woman first and then ask her.
They leave the answer to her own mouth rather than answer for her.
Discovery: what they ask her is not stated in this verse; the passage gives it.

verses.text: When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, “She is my sister,” for he feared to say, “My wife,” thinking, “lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah,” because she was attractive in appearance.

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question to a person (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of'); here the men's inquiry about a man's wife.
Fear here is being afraid of harm from people (tree H3372 1a1 'to fear, be afraid').
Attractive here is pleasing to the senses, to look at (tree H2896 1a 'pleasant, agreeable (to the senses)').
In appearance says that her being attractive lies in how she looked.
The asking is a pursuit: the men seek to learn about his wife.
The fear holds him back from naming her as his wife: it is a refusal to say it.
What they asked about is his wife.
What he feared is that the men would kill him because of Rebekah.
The one said to be attractive is Rebekah.
The fear shows in what he said: that she is his sister.
The men of the place ask; Isaac is the one asked.
Isaac fears the men of the place, and fears for his life at their hands.
Rebekah is the one attractive, and the one whose husband is asked about.
Isaac has settled in Gerar (Gen 26:6) and is among strangers when the men ask.
The men of the place asked Isaac about his wife.
Isaac feared to call her his wife and thought the men might kill him because of her.
He gives her good looks as the reason for the danger he feared.
The men asked; he answered she is his sister; his reason is the fear, and the fear is that they would kill him because of Rebekah, who was attractive.
The question about his wife is what he fears to answer truly.
Discovery: whether the men meant any harm is not stated; the passage is needed.

verses.text: He instructed the first, “ When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, ‘ To whom do you belong? Where are you going? And whose are these ahead of you?’

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts questions to a person (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire'); here questions Jacob expects of Esau.
The asking is a pursuit: Esau is expected to seek to learn who they are and why they come.
The questions are three: to whom the servant belongs, where he is going, and whose the droves ahead are.
Esau is expected to ask; the servant who goes first is the one asked.
Jacob has sent the droves ahead in separate groups with his servants (Gen 32:16) and gives each servant the words for Esau.
Jacob foresees that Esau will ask the first servant three questions.
Esau meets the servant and asks; the servant is then to answer in the words Jacob gives (Gen 32:18).
Jacob prepares for the questioning by giving the questions in full before Esau comes.
Discovery: why Jacob expects these questions of Esau is not stated here; the passage is needed.

verses.text: Then Jacob asked him, “ Please tell me your name.” But he said, “ Why is it that you ask my name?” And there he blessed him.

reference_observations.obs_text: Jacob's asking is a request for something to be made known (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire').
The man's asking is the same verb put back to Jacob as a question about his asking, not a request for information (tree H7592 1a3).
Bless here is the man's act toward Jacob (tree H1288 1a2 'to bless'; Piel 1c).
Tell states the request: that the man make himself known (tree H5046 1a1 'to tell, announce, report', 1a2 'to declare, make known, expound').
Jacob's asking is a pursuit: he seeks the name.
The man's question stands in place of the name: he does not give it.
What Jacob asks for is the man's name.
What the man's question turns on is Jacob's asking of his name.
The one blessed is Jacob.
Jacob asks; the man is the one asked.
The man asks Jacob in return; Jacob is the one questioned.
The man blesses; Jacob is the one blessed.
Jacob has just been given the name Israel (Gen 32:28) when he asks the man's name.
Jacob asked the man to make his name known.
The man answered Jacob's request with a question about it.
The man blessed Jacob there.
Jacob asks for the name; the man asks why; and there he blesses Jacob.
The blessing is given where the name was asked for and not given.
Discovery: why the man withholds his name, and what the blessing gives in its place, the passage must show (Gen 32:30).

verses.text: And a man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, “ What are you seeking?”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question about a person's purpose (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire').
Seek here is seeking to find something or someone (tree H1245 1a1 'to seek to find').
The asking is a pursuit: the man seeks to learn what Joseph is after.
The seeking is a pursuit: Joseph is looking for something.
What the man asks about is Joseph's seeking, his purpose in the fields.
The man asks; Joseph is the one asked.
Joseph is the one seeking; the man who found him is the one who asks about it.
Joseph has been sent by Israel to see how his brothers fare (Gen 37:14) and is alone when the man finds him.
A man who came upon Joseph asked him what he was seeking.
Joseph is taken to be seeking something; the question assumes it.
Joseph is found wandering about; the man then asks what he seeks.
The question draws out the seeking that the verse has not yet named.
Discovery: what Joseph is seeking is not stated in this verse; the passage gives it.

verses.text: And he asked the men of the place, “ Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the roadside?” And they said, “ No cult prostitute has been here.”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question about where someone is (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire').
The asking is a pursuit: he seeks to find out where she is.
What he asks about is the whereabouts of the cult prostitute who had been at the roadside.
The one sent asks; the men of the place are the ones asked and they answer him.
Judah's friend has been sent with the young goat to take back the pledge and has not found her (Gen 38:20).
He asked the people of the place where the woman was.
He asks the men of the place where she is, and they answer that no such woman has been there.
He turns to the people of the place to find her after he could not find her himself.
Discovery: what the men's answer means for the errand, the passage must show (Gen 38:22-23).

verses.text: So he asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, “ Why are your faces downcast today?”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb puts a question about the cause of a state (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for', 1a3 'to enquire').
Downcast, said of faces, is the look of sorrow shown in the face (tree H7451, bad, unpleasant, giving pain, unhappiness).
The asking is a pursuit: Joseph seeks the reason for what he sees.
What he asks about is why their faces are downcast.
What is downcast is their faces, the outward show of their state.
Joseph asks; Pharaoh's officers in custody are the ones asked.
The officers' faces are downcast; Joseph is the one who sees it and asks.
Joseph has seen that they were troubled (Gen 40:6) and they are confined in his master's house.
Joseph asked the officers the reason for their downcast faces.
The officers' faces show sorrow today.
Joseph asks why their faces are downcast, and they answer that they have dreamed and no one interprets (Gen 40:8).
The downcast faces prompt his question: the question names the faces as what he asks about.
Discovery: what lies behind the downcast faces is not stated in this verse; the passage gives their answer (Gen 40:8).

verses.text: And he inquired about their welfare and said, “Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is an inquiry after a person's state (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of'); here after welfare.
Alive here is the father's life, asked of (tree H2416 1 'living, alive').
Still asks whether the life continues after the time that has passed (tree H5750 2a 'still, yet (of continuance or persistence)').
The inquiry is a pursuit: he seeks word of how they and their father are.
What he inquires about is their welfare, and then whether their father is well.
What he asks of the father is whether he lives still.
Joseph asks; his brothers are the ones asked, and their father is the one asked about.
The brothers have just brought the present and bowed to him in his house (Gen 43:26).
Joseph inquired after the brothers' welfare.
Joseph asked whether the father was well and whether he still lived.
He inquires after their welfare, then asks whether their father is well and whether he still lives.
He takes up the brothers' own earlier words about their father.
Discovery: the brothers' answer to both questions is in the next verse; the passage is needed.

verses.text: They replied, “The man questioned us carefully about ourselves and our kindred, saying, ‘Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?’ What we told him was in answer to these questions. Could we in any way know that he would say, ‘Bring your brother down ’?”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is the one of enquiring (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of'); here a close questioning about persons.
Alive here is the state of their father's life, asked of (tree H2416 1 'living, alive').
The verb is to tell, to make known in answer (tree H5046 1a1 'to tell, announce, report').
The verb is to know, here to come to know beforehand (tree H3045 1a1a 'to know, learn to know').
The infinitive before the finite verb makes the questioning close and thorough.
Still asks whether the life continues (tree H5750 2a 'still, yet (of continuance or persistence)').
The infinitive before the finite verb strengthens the question: in any way at all.
His questioning seeks particulars from them: a pursuit of what they know of themselves.
The question implies that they could not have known: a refusal of that knowledge.
What he asked about is themselves and their kindred, and whether they have another brother.
What he asked of their father is whether he still lives.
What they told was in answer to his questions.
What they say they could not know is what he would say next.
What he would say, bring your brother down, is a command to act.
The man questions the brothers, and the question is about their father.
The brothers tell the man what he asked.
The brothers speak of the man and of what he would say.
All of this is the brothers' answer to their father Israel, who has just reproached them for telling the man of another brother (Gen 43:6).
The man questioned them closely about their family.
The man asked whether their father was still alive.
The brothers told him no more than he asked.

verses.text: My lord asked his servants, saying, ‘ Have you a father, or a brother?’

The verb is asking for something as a gift, here a field from her father (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').
The urging is a pursuit: she presses him to act for her.

reference_observations.obs_text: Command here is the Hebrew mouth (H6310): by the Lord's mouth, his word that authorises (tree H6310 1b 'mouth (as organ of speech)').
The verb is asking for something as a gift, here a city (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').

What he asked for is a city.

The verb is the children's question about what the stones mean (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').
The children's asking is a pursuit of what the stones mean.

The verb is asking for something as a gift, here a field from her father (tree H7592 1a1 'to ask, ask for').
The urging is a pursuit: she presses him to act for her.

verses.text: And the angel of the Lord said to him, “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?”

reference_observations.obs_text: The verb is the angel's question put back to Manoah about his asking of the name, not a request for information (tree H7592 1a3 'to enquire, enquire of').

verses.text: Then the woman came and told her husband, “A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name,

verses.text: And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.
